paper_title: Exploring The Empirical Privacy Landscape of Synthetic Data

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Methods for training language models on sensitive data differ in how they balance capability gains against the risk of leaking private information. In this paper, we present a controlled comparison of data-level and training-level interventions for navigating the capability-privacy tradeoff on synthetic medical records with canaries to probe for leakage. Direct finetuning performs best on capability metrics but leads to the most privacy leakage, while DP-SGD reduces leakage at substantial cost to capabilities. Generating synthetic data from these records offers a more favorable balance, particularly when guided by a uniqueness-aware instruction to replace private details. Relative to naive paraphrasing, privacy-aware rewriting improves privacy protection across a variety of different rewriting models. We also find that more capable rewriting models generally reduce the risks of downstream privacy leakage, although held-out fit does not improve monotonically and increased test-time compute yields inconsistent gains. Overall, these results highlight privacy-aware rewriting as a promising direction for achieving a more favorable trade-off between capabilities and empirical privacy compared to other training-level methods, and our evaluation framework supports comparisons of future models and methods.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Modern language models are pretrained and finetuned on large-scale datasets, and their capabilities are closely tied to the scale, diversity, and quality of their training data (Chen et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2024; Wettig et al., 2024; Parmar et al., 2024; Kaplan et al., 2020; Penedo et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2022). For example, models improve in coding capabilities when they have been trained with large amount of coding data (Aryabumi et al., 2025; Seed et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2024). Similarly, adapting language models to high-stakes domains often requires access to large quantity of sensitive records. Directly training on such data can raise privacy and safety concerns, as language models can memorize training examples and reveal sensitive information during inference (Carlini et al., 2021; Nasr et al., 2025). Such information may include personally identifiable health data or knowledge relevant to biological misuse (Maini et al., 2026; OBrien et al., 2026). Existing approaches for mitigating privacy leakage can be broadly divided into two categories based on the stage at which privacy protection is introduced. Data-level methods modify or replace the training data to reduce the exposure of sensitive information. For example, synthetic data generation uses generative model to produce records that preserve useful semantic information while removing sensitive details. Training-level methods, by contrast, modify the optimization procedure. An example is differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) (Abadi et al., 2016), which limits the influence of individual training examples and provides formal privacy guarantees. Prior work has shown that stronger privacy protection often comes at the cost of reduced model utility, while methods that better preserve model capabilities may increase the risk of privacy leakage Work done at MATS. Right: Results for finetuning gpt-oss-20b, with each axis averaging ranks across two privacy and two capability metrics. Higher ranks indicate less privacy leakage and greater capabilities. Arrows connect rewriting to privacy-aware rewriting, which improves both privacy and capability. (Li et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2025). However, existing studies typically evaluate individual privacypreserving methods or focus on either privacy or utility in isolation. Consequently, those data-level and training-level methods have not been systematically compared within controlled setting in terms of both model capability and privacy leakage. In this work, we conduct controlled study of the relationship between model capability and privacy leakage when training on sensitive data, which is illustrated in Figure 1. We first construct corpus of realistic synthetic medical records (Walonoski et al., 2018). While we do not have access to the training datasets of the pretrained models, we believe that there is no overlap with our newly generated synthetic dataset and their pretraining dataset. This controlled setup allows us to attribute privacy leakage to the data introduced during our experiments, rather than to prior exposure during pretraining. We apply range of methods to finetune models and evaluate each method along two dimensions: privacy leakage and model capability. By visualizing performance along these dimensions, we characterize the trade-off between privacy and utility, identify methods that achieve more favorable balance, and provide deeper understanding of how different privacy-preserving approaches affect model behavior. Our results demonstrate that synthetic data through rewriting provides promising path toward improving model capability with only minor reductions in privacy protection. We find that the specific rewriting strategy is crucial to achieving favorable trade-offs, and this trade-off scales nicely with the quality of the synthetic data generation model, but increasing test-time compute during rewriting does not monotonically improve the trade-off. Our canary-duplication experiments further show that repeated exposure generally increases privacy leakage, although DP-SGD and privacyaware rewriting remain resistant at high duplication levels. Moreover, training on five independent rewrites for one epoch provides no advantage over training on one rewrite for five epochs, despite requiring additional generation. Finally, we compare data-level evaluation with measurements after finetuning. LLM-judged privacy strongly correlates with verbatim privacy metrics (ρ = 0.89), whereas judged quality does not predict improved capability (ρ = 0.64), showing that data-level metrics cannot reliably replace downstream evaluations of finetuned models.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Memorization in Language Models Training data memorization means model retains information tied to specific training examples rather than learning generalizable patterns. Prior work evaluates memorization through extraction attacks. Carlini et al. (2019) introduce canaries in the training data and measure the extraction of these sequences. Subsequent attacks demonstrated that language models can reproduce verbatim training examples, including personally identifiable information (Carlini et al., 2021). Although much of this literature studies pretraining, models can also 2 memorize examples introduced during finetuning. Susceptibility to membership-inference and extraction attacks varies across full-model, output-head, and adapter-based finetuning (Mireshghallah et al., 2022). Large-scale analyses further found that memorization increases with model capacity and example duplication (Carlini et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2022). Repeated exposure is also an important factor. Kandpal et al. (2022) found that an example becomes more likely to be regenerated as its training frequency increases and that dataset deduplication can substantially reduce extraction risk. Controlled studies further show that memorization depends on an examples frequency relative to the corpus size and on when it appears during training (Wei et al., 2026). Exact duplicates are not required for this effect: approximate copies can still induce memorization (Shilov et al., 2026). Memorization is also not limited to exact reproduction. Training information may remain recoverable even when exact reproduction is prevented (Ippolito et al., 2023), and certain methods can scalably quantify near-verbatim extraction (Cooper et al., 2026a). The degree of verbatim memorization does not necessarily predict whether information can be extracted through natural-language questions (Sander et al., 2026). Question-based evaluations must also account for lexical clues that may make the expected answer easier to reconstruct (Luo et al., 2026). Following these distinctions, we evaluate prefix-based completion and question-based recall separately (Cooper et al., 2026b). Mitigating Memorization and Privacy Leakage De-identification mitigates privacy leakage by detecting and removing predefined categories of protected health information, such as names, addresses, and identification numbers (Norgeot et al., 2020). Other methods replace detected identifiers with realistic fictional surrogates to retain the structure and utility of the text (Carrell et al., 2013). Nevertheless, these methods can reduce but do not necessarily eliminate information leakage from finetuned language models (Lukas et al., 2023). More broadly, in some circumstances, personal attributes may be inferred from contextual clues even when direct identifiers are absent (Staab et al., 2024). Recent LLM-based anonymization methods therefore consider contextual distinctiveness and replace details according to their re-identification risk (Staab et al., 2025). Our comparison between PII scrubbing and privacy-aware rewriting reflects this distinction between redaction and removing contextually distinctive information. Because the canaries are not conventional identifiers, this tests whether these defenses protect against personal information that is not traditional PII. Privacy-preserving training provides complementary line of defense. DP-SGD bounds the influence of individual training examples through per-example gradient clipping, calibrated noise, and privacy accounting (Abadi et al., 2016). Subsequent work has adapted differential privacy to parameter-efficient language-model finetuning (Yu et al., 2021). Differential privacy has also been applied to synthetic-text generation through privately finetuned generators (Yue et al., 2023) and through private selection procedures using foundation-model APIs (Xie et al., 2024). Synthetic or rewritten text is not inherently private, however, and membership information may remain detectable in generated corpora (Meeus et al., 2025). Goldfish follows an empirical rather than formal approach, masking selected next-token targets from the training loss to reduce verbatim memorization (Hans et al., 2024). In contrast to studies primarily concerned with releasing synthetic datasets, we directly compare preprocessing and training defenses by measuring both privacy leakage and capability in the resulting finetuned models. Our one-to-one rewriting methods do not provide formal differential-privacy guarantee; their privacy effects are evaluated empirically.

sections.title: 3 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: 3.1 DATASET AND CANARY CONSTRUCTION We use Synthea (Walonoski et al., 2018) to generate synthetic patient records that serve as controlled proxy for private clinical corpus. Because the records are generated specifically for our experiments, overlap with model pretraining data is unlikely, reducing pretraining contamination as confounder. Each record contains synthetic patient demographics and identifiers, including name, address, SSN, and date of birth, together with active problems and current medications. From the generated population, we use 5,000 records for training and reserve disjoint held-out evaluation set. Following established canary-based privacy leakage evaluation (Carlini et al., 2019), we construct 100 unique canary records in the same format and length as the non-canary training records. For each canary, we jointly sample the demographics, address, problem list, and existing medications 3 from single non-canary training record, assign fabricated identity, and append plausible, newly coined medication name as the planted secret. This medication name is fully synthetic and is few tokens (e.g., Mabsartinib in Table 1). We divide the canaries equally into five groups and insert them at multiplicities of 1, 4, 16, 32, and 64, respectively. This produces 5,000 + 20(1 + 4 + 16 + 32 + 64) = 7,340 training instances, comprising 5,000 non-canary records and 2,340 canaries.

sections.title: 3.2 BASELINES AND PRIVACY-PRESERVING METHODS
sections.content: We compare six experimental settings based on the same pretrained model and evaluate them using the same privacy and utility metrics. All trained conditions start from the same corpus but differ in either the training objective or the preprocessing applied to the corpus. No finetuning We evaluate the pretrained model without any exposure to the training corpus. Direct finetuning We directly finetune the model on the training corpus without privacy-specific preprocessing or modifications to the training objective. PII scrubbing Before finetuning, we process every training record using the OpenAI Privacy Filter (de Bourcy et al., 2026). Detected identifiers, including names, telephone numbers, emails, and private addresses, are replaced with placeholders. We finetune the model on this redacted corpus. DP-SGD We train only the LoRA adapters using example-level DP-SGD (Abadi et al., 2016), clipping per-example gradients to = 1 and adding Gaussian noise calibrated to (ϵ, δ) with δ = 105. We use Poisson sampling with an expected lot size of 512. Our main comparison uses ϵ = 8. To study the privacy budget, we also train with ϵ {16, 32, 64}. Goldfish Goldfish modifies the training objective while leaving the input records unchanged (Hans et al., 2024). deterministic, context-dependent mask excludes approximately 1/k of eligible token targets from the loss; we use = 4. The masked tokens remain visible in context but do not contribute to the training loss. Rewriting language model rewrites every training record, including each duplicated canary copy, while preserving its clinical content. We then finetune the model on the rewritten corpus. Privacy-aware rewriting This condition follows the rewriting pipeline described above but adds uniqueness-aware prompt to instruct the model to replace rare details that could single out patient with plausible fictional alternatives while retaining common clinical information. The rewriting instructions for both conditions are shown in Table 1. 3.3 MODEL AND TRAINING CONFIGURATION We evaluate all methods using Qwen3.5-4B-Base (Qwen Team, 2026) and gpt-oss-20b (Agarwal et al., 2025). We select these open-weight models because they differ in model family and scale, allowing us to examine whether the observed trends persist across target models. Except for the no finetuning method, we train LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022) for two epochs with rank = 16, scaling parameter α = 32, zero dropout, and all supported linear layers as target modules. We use AdamW with constant learning rate of 2 104, batch size of 4, maximum sequence length of 1,024 tokens, and bfloat16 precision. All experiments use random seed 0, and the training records are processed in fixed order. Qwen is finetuned directly on the training records using causal language modeling, whereas gpt-oss is finetuned using its native chat format. 3.4 PRIVACY AND CAPABILITY METRICS We evaluate privacy leakage using verbatim perplexity and semantic perplexity. visualization of each metric is provided in Table 2. For each canary, the verbatim probe provides the record prefix ending immediately before the planted medication and measures the perplexity of the coined medication. The semantic probe asks question about the fabricated patient that is constructed so that the coined medication is the unique correct answer. Because each coined medication appears only in copies of its associated canary, assigning it high likelihood under either probe provides evidence that the model memorized the planted medication from the training data. For each probe, we average the medications token-level log-likelihood across the canaries and exponentiate the negative mean to obtain perplexity. Lower values indicate better capability for both metrics.

sections.title: 4 RESULTS
sections.content: As shown in Figures 1 and 8, the methods follow broadly downward trend, indicating that stronger protection against privacy leakage generally comes at the cost of lower capability. Direct finetuning achieves the highest capability improvements for both models and receives the second-lowest privacy rank for gpt-oss-20b. In contrast, no finetuning expectedly achieves the highest privacy rank but the lowest capability rank because the model is exposed to neither the canaries nor the dataset. 5 PII scrubbing alone also ranks poorly on privacy relative to most other methods. In our zero-shot application of PII scrubbing model, private information, such as coined medications, remains unredacted, illustrating limitation of this baseline in protecting from leakage of non-identifier facts. Although not consistent pattern across our experiments, PII scrubbing alone ranks below direct finetuning in Figure 1; possible explanation is that standardized placeholders reduce surface-form variation, making the remaining content easier to learn. DP-SGD achieves relatively high privacy rank but lower capability rank than most other trained methods. Goldfish retains high capability rank but performs poorly in privacy, indicating that its token-masking objective does not sufficiently protect canary information in this setting. Rewriting-based methods generally occupy intermediate regions of both panels, providing relatively balanced privacycapability trade-offs. For both target models, privacy-aware rewriting achieves better privacy and capability ranks than standard rewriting. For rewriting, we use GPT-5.5 and Qwen3.5-4B as closed-source and open-weight rewrite models. Across both target models, GPT5.5 achieves higher privacy ranks but lower capability ranks than Qwen3.5-4B, suggesting that its stronger privacy protection comes at some cost to capability. However, rewriting-based methods require additional computation because each training record must pass through generative model before finetuning. The resulting privacy and capability gains must be considered alongside this preprocessing cost. We further analyze rewriting in Section 4.2. 4.1 CANARY DUPLICATION We examine how canary duplication affects privacy using five disjoint groups of 20 canaries, inserted at different frequencies (1, 4, 16, 32, and 64). Figure 2 and Figure 11 report verbatim and semantic perplexity across these duplication factors. Because each duplication level contains different group of canaries, differences across levels can reflect both duplication and intrinsic canary difficulty. The no finetuning model provides reference for this difficulty. For example, its higher perplexity at 32 indicates that this group is intrinsically more difficult. We therefore interpret each trained condition relative to the no finetuning reference at the same duplication level. Across both target models, PII scrubbing generally tracks direct finetuning and produces low perplexity at higher duplication levels, indicating that removing direct identifiers provides little protection against privacy leakage. In contrast, DP-SGD and GPT-5.5 privacy-aware rewriting maintain higher perplexity, even at high duplication levels. Goldfish is generally less sensitive to increasing duplication than direct finetuning. This relative stability is consistent with its deterministic, contextdependent masking. Because identical copies receive the same mask, duplicating record does not add new training signals for tokens excluded from the loss. 4.2 REWRITING Previous results show that rewriting-based methods provide relatively balanced privacycapability trade-offs. We therefore compare rewrite models from different model families, ablating the size, amount of test-time compute, and rewrite strategy to examine how much the exact rewriting details affect this trade-off. Scaling Rewrite Model Capabilities improves Privacy As shown in Figure 3, adding the privacy-aware instruction improves the privacy rank for every rewrite model comparison shown in both panels. Capability improves in most cases. GPT-5.5 achieves the highest privacy rank in both target-model panels. Overall, larger rewrite models generally achieve higher privacy ranks than smaller rewrite models, particularly when given the privacy-aware instruction. This suggests that more capable rewrite models are better able to identify and replace distinctive details. We further examine privacy-aware rewriting using several rewrite models, as shown in Figure 4. Across both target models, later GPT-5 variants consistently achieve better privacy protection, whereas capability does not improve monotonically. Capability generally increases from GPT-5.1 through GPT-5.4. These results suggest that using stronger rewrite model can improve privacy protection without guaranteeing corresponding improvement in capability. As shown in Figure 4, increasing reasoning effort does not monotonically improve either rank, and the best setting depends on the target model. Nevertheless, enabling reasoning generally provides more favorable trade-off than the no-reasoning setting. These results suggest that some reasoning is beneficial, but increasing the reasoning budget does not consistently improve performance. Summary-Based Rewriting Summarization may improve privacy by discarding record-specific details while retaining useful clinical information. We therefore evaluate rewriting technique that first summarizes each record and then expands the summary into new record to control for formatting. We compare standard summarization with privacy-aware variant that applies our uniquenessaware instruction. The effect on privacy leakage varies across models, suggesting no consistent improvement in the privacycapability trade-off. Independent Rewrites versus Repeated Training Training for multiple epochs repeatedly exposes the model to the same rewritten records. We therefore compare two settings: training on one rewrite for five epochs and training for one epoch on five independently generated rewrites. As shown in Figure 6, the two radar profiles largely overlap, indicating similar performance across the evaluated metrics. The one-rewrite, five-epoch condition performs slightly better overall, suggesting that independent rewrites provide no clear advantage despite their additional generation cost. 8 Figure 6: Comparison of five independent rewrites trained for one epoch each and single rewrite trained for five epochs. In both panels, the GPT-5.5 single-rewrite, five-epoch condition is normalized to 1; all other values are reported as ratios to this reference. Higher values indicate better performance on every axis. Figure 7: Comparison of LLM-judged scores with measured outcomes using Qwen3.5-4B-Base as the target model. Left: judged quality versus capability. Right: judged privacy versus verbatim perplexity. Point labels indicate the GPT-series rewriter and reasoning-effort setting. 4.3 PRIVACY AND CAPABILITY METRICS FOR DATA Our primary evaluation finetunes target model on each rewritten corpus and measures privacy and capability. We also examine whether an LLM can predict these outcomes by inspecting the rewritten data alone. We use GPT-5.6-sol with xhigh reasoning to compare each original record with its corresponding rewrite and assign separate privacy and quality scores. To reduce confounding from cross-family stylistic differences, we restrict this analysis to GPT-series rewrite models. As shown in Figure 7, judged privacy strongly correlates with verbatim perplexity (Spearmans ρ = 0.89). Because higher verbatim perplexity indicates less privacy leakage, the judge successfully tracks the relative privacy ordering of the rewritten corpora. In contrast, judged quality correlates negatively with measured capability (ρ = 0.64), indicating that rewrites rated as higher quality do 9 not necessarily produce more capable finetuned models. Thus, LLM judging may provide useful secondary signal for privacy risk, but it cannot replace direct capability evaluation.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented controlled evaluation of the privacycapability trade-off in language-model finetuning using synthetic medical-record corpus. Among the evaluated methods, privacy-aware rewriting achieves the most balanced overall trade-off. Stronger rewrite models generally provided better privacy protection, although capability and the benefits of additional reasoning effort were not monotonic. We also find that LLM-judged privacy tracks verbatim leakage, whereas judged data quality does not reliably predict model capability. These findings establish privacy-aware rewriting as promising direction for balancing privacy and capability.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used generative AI tools to help polish the writing and to draft parts of the text, such as figure captions. The research ideas in this work are our own and did not come from AI tools. We reviewed and verified all AI-assisted text. The language models that serve as rewriters and as judge in our experiments are part of the studied methods and are described in Section 3. We take full responsibility for the content of this work, including any text, claims, or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT All data are fully synthetic: patient records are generated with Synthea from fixed seed, and canaries are built by seeded code, so the full training corpus can be regenerated. Both fine-tuned models are open-weight (Qwen3.5-4B-Base and gpt-oss-20b), and every fine-tuned model uses the same LoRA setup (rank 16, α=32, learning rate 2104, 2 epochs, 1,024-token sequences, seed 0); DP-SGD adds per-example clipping (norm 1.0) and Gaussian noise calibrated to ε=8, δ=105. API rewriters and the LLM judge are called with fixed model identifiers and reasoning-effort settings. Prompts, hyperparameters, and metric definitions are given in the appendix. sections.content: A.1 PRIVACYCAPABILITY TRADE-OFFS Figures 9 and 10 report the individual metric values for each method. Compared with direct finetuning, privacy-aware rewriting shows only small differences in the capability metrics but substantially higher verbatim and semantic perplexity, indicating reduced privacy leakage. Figure 8: Privacycapability trade-offs across methods. Arrows connect rewriting to privacyaware rewriting for the same rewrite model. Figure 9: Privacycapability trade-offs across methods. Lines connect rewriting to privacy-aware rewriting for the same rewrite model. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals. Figure 10: Privacycapability trade-offs across methods. Lines connect rewriting to privacyaware rewriting for the same rewrite model. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals. A.2 CANARY DUPLICATION Figure 11: Canary privacy leakage across duplication factors. Rows show Qwen3.5-4B-Base and gpt-oss-20b; columns show semantic perplexity. Higher values indicate less privacy leakage, and error bars show 95% confidence intervals over 20 canaries per group. 15 Figure 12: Privacycapability trade-offs for privacy-aware rewriting with Qwen3.5-4B-Base as the target model. The left shows different rewriting models, while the right shows different amounts of reasoning. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals. A.3 SCALING REWRITE MODEL CAPABILITIES Figure 12 shows that, with Qwen3.5-4B as the target model, stronger rewrite models generally improve privacy protection but do not consistently improve the target models capability. Figures 13 and 14 show similar trends when using semantic perplexity and inverse medication perplexity as the privacy and capability metrics. Figure 13: Privacycapability trade-offs for privacy-aware rewriting with gpt-oss-20b as the target model. The left shows different rewriting models, while the right shows different amounts of reasoning. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals. 16 Figure 14: Privacycapability trade-offs for privacy-aware rewriting with Qwen3.5-4B-Base as the target model. The left shows different rewriting models, while the right shows different amounts of reasoning. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals. A.4 SCALING REWRITE TEST-TIME COMPUTE Figure 12 shows that, with Qwen3.5-4B as the target model, increasing reasoning effort does not consistently improve privacy or capability, although reasoning-enabled settings generally provide better privacy protection than the none setting. Figures 13 and 14 show similar trends when using semantic perplexity and inverse medication perplexity as the privacy and capability metrics. A.5 SUMMARY-BASED REWRITING As shown in Figure 15, the effects of summarization remain model-dependent. Held-out record perplexity may partly reflect the formatting guidance provided during expansion, since the auxiliary examples share similar structure with the held-out records. The effect on verbatim perplexity also varies across target models. Overall, privacy-aware summary-based rewriting remains practical alternative to privacy-aware rewriting without summarization when the finetuning compute budget is limited. A.6 INDEPENDENT REWRITES VERSUS REPEATED TRAINING Figure 16 shows that, for rewriting, training on one rewrite per record for five epochs outperforms training on five independent rewrites per record for one epoch. A.7 PRIVACY AND CAPABILITY METRICS FOR DATA Figure 17 compares judged quality with medication perplexity and judged privacy with semantic perplexity. The results support the same conclusion: LLM-judged privacy tracks measured privacy, whereas judged quality does not reliably predict model capability. Figures 18 and 19 show similar trends with gpt-oss-20b as the target model. A.8 CORRELATION OF PRIVACY METRICS We examine the correlation between verbatim and semantic perplexity as shown in Figure 20, grouping results by verbatim perplexity. For Qwen3.5-4B-Base, the correlation is 0.84, but the correlation 17 Figure 15: Privacycapability trade-offs for privacy-aware rewriting with and without summarization step. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals. Figure 16: Comparison of five independent rewrites trained for one epoch each and single rewrite trained for five epochs. In both panels, the GPT-5.5 single-rewrite, five-epoch condition is normalized to 1; all other values are reported as ratios to this reference. Higher values indicate better performance on every axis. is 0.39 below verbatim perplexity of 100 and 0.98 above this threshold. For gpt-oss-20b, the correlation is 0.85, but the correlation is 0.05 below verbatim perplexity of 100 and 0.68 above this threshold. These results support reporting both metrics, as they provide complementary measurements of privacy leakage, particularly when verbatim perplexity is low. A.9 CORRELATION OF CAPABILITY METRICS We also examine the correlation between held-out record perplexity and medication perplexity as shown in Figure 21. For Qwen3.5-4B-Base, the correlation is 0.60, but the correlation is 0.52 when held-out record perplexity is below 2.5 and 0.44 above this threshold. For gpt-oss-20b, the correlation is 0.81, but the correlation is 0.90 when held-out record perplexity is below 2.5 and 0.75 18 Figure 17: Comparison of LLM-judged scores with measured outcomes using Qwen3.5-4BBase as the target model. Left: judged quality versus capability. Right: judged privacy versus verbatim perplexity. Point labels indicate the GPT-series rewriter and reasoning-effort setting. Figure 18: Comparison of LLM-judged scores with measured outcomes using gpt-oss-20b as the target model. Left: judged quality versus capability. Right: judged privacy versus verbatim perplexity. Point labels indicate the GPT-series rewriter and reasoning-effort setting. above this threshold. These results support reporting both metrics, as they capture different aspects of model capability. A.10 PROBABILITY OF GENERATING THE COINED MEDICATION Perplexity is the inverse of the models average per-token probability, which makes differences between methods hard to read. We therefore also report the probability that model generates the coined medication given the record up to it: the product of the models probabilities for the medications tokens. This is the chance that single sampled continuation reproduces the coined medication. 19 Figure 19: Comparison of LLM-judged scores with measured outcomes using gpt-oss-20b as the target model. Left: judged quality versus capability. Right: judged privacy versus verbatim perplexity. Point labels indicate the GPT-series rewriter and reasoning-effort setting. Figure 22 shows this probability against the number of times each canary appeared in training. After direct finetuning on Qwen3.5-4B-Base, coined medication seen once is generated 16% of the time and one seen 64 times 99% of the time; PII scrubbing follows closely (7% to 94%), and Goldfish levels off at 3040%. gpt-oss-20b needs duplication before it memorizes: after direct finetuning, coined medication seen once is generated about once in 37,000 samples, rising to 69% at 64. Rewriting with GPT-5.5 lowers the probability to between 109 and 103, and DP-SGD stays on the no finetuning floor, below 1011, at every duplication level. Under privacy-aware rewriting with GPT-5.5 the typical canary also sits at the floor; the jumps at 16 and 64 each come from single leaked canary (on Qwen3.5-4B-Base at 16, one canary is generated 0.5% of the time and the next only 1011 of the time). A.11 LIKELIHOOD-BASED EXPOSURE OF CANARY MEDICATIONS To assess how strongly model favors planted medication over alternative completions, we complement our perplexity measurements with the exposure metric introduced by Carlini et al. (2019). For each canary, we condition on the original record prefix ending immediately before its medication name and score candidate names using summed token log probabilities. The candidate set contains the planted name and 6,300 unplanted alternatives drawn from the same coined-name space, excluding the other 99 planted medications. If the true name ranks among these 6,301 candidates, its exposure is = log2(6,301) log2 r. We report mean exposure across the 100 canaries and the proportion whose planted name ranks first. Rewriting reduces exposure on both target models, and privacy-aware instructions further reduce it for both rewriters. The reduction is larger with GPT-5.5 than with Qwen3.5-4B.
